title_original: Denis Boulze and the Sweet Life of Clichés

blocks.text: “Images don’t belong to us. Proust’s madeleine is the same for everyone.” Set as the epigraph of Clichés (in French, the word means both a stereotype and a photograph), Denis Boulze’s line has the candor of a confession slipped backstage, between two takes. The photographer knows the recipe, having served it for years in the pages of Vogue , Silhouette and Milk , for Hermès and JM Weston: a face, a hand, a shaft of light, and the reader’s memory does the rest. A proven recipe. On Roxane Moreau’s podcast Dans le bain , recorded on the evening of his first solo exhibition, Denis Boulze readily speaks of his “candy images.” Sweet, then, and a little guilty.

The taste goes back a long way. The son of a photographer, Denis Boulze started as an intern at 16 at Studio Rouchon in Paris, where he later assisted Sarah Moon, Jan Walter, Sofia and Mauro. A tough school, and a lucky draw. In the acknowledgments, he gives his father his due, the man who passed on to him “a taste for the image” and taught him “to see.” The rest reads like a travel journal, since this “beautiful profession,” he writes, “has always been a pretext for me to travel, meet new people and live experiences that have deeply enriched me.” A craftsman’s courtesy, which also salutes his agent, the formidable Florence Moll, and the printers David Dahan and Luis Escudero, thanks to whom color printing has, as the artist puts it, “today become an essential part of my work.”

So why a book? Weariness? Remorse? A big spring cleaning? On his professional profile, Denis Boulze once let out this cry from the heart: “Help, fashion! Seeing the same photographers, the same stylists, the same models over and over, I’m getting a little bored.” Clichés answers with the simplest gesture: opening the archive boxes, cutting, pasting, layering. The bags, the bottles, the logos evaporate. What remains are bodies, gestures, postures. Claire Luna, winner of the 2025 AICA-France Élisabeth Couturier Prize for art criticism, sees in it, in her opening text, “almost a visual coming out,” and extends the metaphor all the way to the closet: the curtain has risen, “but something still lies coiled.”

What you find inside: 16 faces striped with shadow, 16 hands raised as if to stop traffic, a white dove above a red and orange puddle, starfish clinging to an ear. A moodboard? Almost. Denis Boulze works in diptychs and strips, slipping a tab of red or khaki-green paper between two prints, the way one dog-ears a page in a cookbook. A woman’s profile answers an antique plaster head; two long-necked bottles bathe in a day-for-night blue, a Morandi gone to the movies; a transparent dress floats against black, a dry cleaner’s ghost. The painted lips, for their part, are doubled, like a rubber stamp pressed twice (Blumenfeld and Man Ray have been here before).

The strength of the whole lies in its softness. Everything here belongs to reminiscence, a tune hummed without knowing who wrote it, hence the title Claire Luna chose, “Comme une chanson populaire” (Like a Popular Song). Denis Boulze embraces this shared memory, which he also claims for his series “Portrait de famille” (Family Portrait), made every summer in a former chestnut-drying hut in the Cévennes: a series “very dear to me,” he wrote, “although it is unfinished and will probably remain so forever,” meant to preserve “this parenthesis of our lives which, in my opinion, resembles a gentle poetry.” Clichés shares this slow tempo, like a family album whose members happen to be strangers.

Designed by Line Célo and printed by LONGO in Bolzano, the book has the restraint of a portfolio laid on a table at a festival portfolio review. Generous white space, airy sequences, color used sparingly and all the more precious for it. Some plates read like a catalog of forms, plaster spheres and half-moons in a Bauhaus vein; others keep a touch of glamour that Denis Boulze owns without false modesty. One could see this as a limitation. One could also read it as a form of honesty: the photographer lays out his alphabet, worn letters included, and leaves readers to recognize their own words in it.

Which leaves the question of authorship. To whom does a hand resting on a cheek belong, an eye under makeup, a glass of milk on a dark table? To everyone, answers the epigraph. To whoever looks, the book corrects. Denis Boulze has known this since childhood, and closes his acknowledgments with his father, thanked for a lifelong lesson: “the importance of looking and cultivating my eye.”
Denis Boulze’s Clichés , with a text by Claire Luna, is self-published and available for €40. To buy the book, contact Denis Boulze directly via his Instagram account .
